claims.text: The target particles are initially solid, equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Equiatomic composition gives the target alloy high configurational entropy.
Multi-element atomic disorder creates local variations in atomic configuration.
Multi-element atomic disorder creates significant local variations in bond strength.
Multi-element atomic disorder creates local lattice strain.
Local variations in bonding environment and strain produce lower melting-onset temperatures in some regions of the HEA nanoparticles.
Local variations in bonding environment and strain cause melting to begin at spatially different temperatures within individual HEA nanoparticles.
The Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will have a broader premelting interval than comparable bimetallic nanoparticles.
Different regions of an individual Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticle will begin melting at different temperatures.
Chemically simpler bimetallic nanoparticles such as Fe–Co exhibit a sharper and more spatially uniform melting transition.
Spatially resolved in situ thermal microscopy can be used during controlled heating to monitor premelting and melting within individual particles.
The HEA and bimetallic samples should be compared at identical heating rates and similar particle sizes and dispersions.
Surface effects are significant for particles in the stated 5–50 nm diameter range.
Cooling rate can significantly alter the microstructure and phases produced from a high-entropy-alloy melt.
Rapid cooling consolidates the Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu solid solution.
The extent and temperature range of melting heterogeneity may depend on synthesis conditions, particle-size distribution, and defect density.
Failure of the HEA particles to show broader and more spatially heterogeneous premelting than the bimetallic control would falsify the proposed disorder-based explanation.
